issues.legal_issue: A localized roof collapse, without evidence that a substantial part of the building is unsafe or unfit for habitation, does not establish a ground for eviction based on the building’s condition.
material_facts: The tenant occupied four ground-floor rooms used as an office; the landlord occupied a separate room on the first floor.
The roof of one room in the rear of the leased premises had fallen down, but no other damage to the building was noticed.
The tenant replaced the roof after obtaining permission from the Rent Controller, and the landlord had consented to that permission.
The landlord did not seek eviction on the building-condition ground until after losing before the Rent Controller and appealing.
There was no evidence that the collapse showed that the whole building or a substantial part of it was damaged, unsafe, or unfit for habitation.
issues.conclusion: The isolated roof collapse did not establish that the building had become unsafe and unfit for human habitation, so eviction on that ground was not justified. The fact that repairs do not necessarily extinguish an already accrued cause of action does not make every instance of damage sufficient to establish such a cause of action.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(3)(a)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 requires evidence that the building, viewed as a whole, has become unsafe and unfit for human habitation; damage to one part is not by itself sufficient unless it supports that conclusion about the building or a substantial part of it. Section 12 concerns a tenant’s permission to carry out repairs. Balbir Singh v. Hari Ram and Chander Mohini v. Jiva Singh concerned the effect of repairs on a cause of action that had arisen; they did not hold that every instance of damage creates such a cause of action. Sardarni Sampurna Kaur v. Sant Singh involved a substantial portion of the composite building being unsafe and unfit, and was distinguished.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_case and localized_roof_collapse and no_other_building_damage and no_evidence_of_substantial_building_unfitness

predicates.tenant_eviction_case: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the basis that the building was unsafe or unfit for habitation.
predicates.localized_roof_collapse: The roof in one room collapsed, and the damage was confined to that room.
predicates.no_other_building_damage: No other damage to the building was identified.
predicates.no_evidence_of_substantial_building_unfi: The evidence did not show that the building, or a substantial part of it, had become unsafe or unfit for habitation.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks eviction based on a building’s condition, a localized roof collapse with no other damage and no evidence of substantial building unfitness does not establish the asserted eviction ground.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court is not justified in setting aside concurrent factual findings against eviction when its decision rests on mistaken assumptions and the evidence does not establish the required condition of the building.
material_facts: The Rent Controller found against the landlord on the building-condition ground, and the Appellate Authority concurred.
The High Court reversed those findings in revision and ordered eviction.
The High Court treated the roof collapse in one room as sufficient by itself and also mistakenly assumed that a wall had crumbled.
The expert evidence described the condition of three outer walls; the fourth wall was common to the room and an adjoining room.
The record showed no damage beyond the roof collapse in one room and did not establish that a substantial part of the building was unsafe or unfit for habitation.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the concurrent findings and directing eviction on the evidence and assumptions before it.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that the High Court’s revisional intervention was unjustified because it proceeded on mistaken factual assumptions and treated an isolated roof collapse as sufficient without evidence supporting a finding that the building or a substantial part of it was unsafe and unfit for habitation under Section 13(3)(a)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949. The court distinguished Balbir Singh v. Hari Ram, Chander Mohini v. Jiva Singh, and Sardarni Sampurna Kaur v. Sant Singh because their facts did not support the High Court’s conclusion in this case.

predicates.tenant_eviction_revision: A landlord challenged an adverse eviction decision in revision, and the matter came before the Supreme Court on appeal.
predicates.concurrent_findings_against_unsafe_build: The first-instance and appellate decision-makers both found against eviction on the asserted building-condition ground.
predicates.revisional_court_relied_on_mistaken_assu: The revisional court relied on a factual assumption about damage that the evidence did not support.
predicates.evidence_not_supporting_substantial_buil: The evidence did not establish that the building or a substantial part of it was unsafe or unfit for habitation.

issues.definition: When a revisional court overturns concurrent findings against eviction based on a mistaken assumption and evidence that does not establish substantial building unfitness, its eviction order is not justified.

issues.legal_issue: An additional-accommodation ground that was not canvassed before the High Court and was not seriously pressed before the appellate authority cannot support eviction in the appeal.
material_facts: The landlord had originally sought eviction on additional-accommodation and other grounds, as well as on a later-added building-condition ground.
The additional-accommodation ground was not canvassed before the High Court.
The appellate authority observed that the building-condition ground was the only ground seriously pressed; the additional-accommodation point was raised only incidentally.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s additional-accommodation contention had no merit in the appeal and did not provide a basis to uphold eviction.
issues.legal_principle: The court declined to rely on the additional-accommodation ground because it had not been canvassed before the High Court and had not been seriously pressed before the appellate authority; the judgment identifies no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this conclusion.

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: A tenant appealed against an order directing eviction.
predicates.additional_accommodation_ground_not_canv: The landlord did not argue the additional-accommodation ground before the High Court.
predicates.additional_accommodation_ground_not_seri: The landlord did not seriously press that ground before the lower appellate decision-maker.

issues.definition: In a tenant’s eviction appeal, an additional-accommodation ground that was neither canvassed before the High Court nor seriously pressed below cannot support eviction.
